ASTRA — Production-Ready, Modular, Research-
Grade Specification for NASA Space Apps 2026
Executive summary
ASTRA should be built as a production-shaped research prototype of an Earth-independent crew-
health intelligence platform, not as a conventional health dashboard and not as an autonomous “AI
doctor.” The official 2026 NASA Space Apps challenge asks teams to create software that gathers astronaut
health indicators and helps astronauts evaluate and act on their health during long-duration missions,
explicitly citing radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, immune changes, bone loss,
cardiovascular events, and behavioral-health problems.  Your uploaded challenge guide independently
identifies this challenge as a particularly strong fit for personalized baselines, offline operation,
communication-delay simulation, anomaly detection, and a Crew Health Agent. fileciteturn0file0
The strongest technical framing is therefore:
ASTRA is a multimodal, offline-capable Crew Health Intelligence and Mission-Control
platform that creates a continuously updated visual health twin of each crew member,
detects deviations from personal baselines, explains the evidence, retrieves trusted
space-health knowledge, and synchronizes crew-health cases with Earth despite
communication delay or blackout.
That framing closely matches the direction of NASA's own exploration-medical research. NASA's Exploration
Medical Capability work describes a future clinical decision-support architecture that combines multiple
health, environmental, behavioral, wearable, laboratory, and vehicle data streams because deep-space
communication delays require progressively more Earth-independent medical operations. NASA's
exploration EHR work likewise identifies asynchronous store-and-forward communication, onboard access
to crew-health data, and increasing autonomy as important capabilities beyond low Earth orbit. 
The winning version of ASTRA is not the version with the largest number of disconnected AI features.
It is the version that demonstrates one extraordinary end-to-end scenario in which every subsystem works
together:
sensor/simulator → validated telemetry → real-time Mission Control → 3D astronaut health twin →
personalized anomaly detection → evidence/explainability → cited RAG knowledge → constrained
Crew Health Agent → communication-delay queue → Earth review → complete audit trail.
NASA research into Earth-independent operations now explicitly discusses integrated data systems
combining multiple streams with AI-supported/agentic clinical decision support, which gives ASTRA's
system-of-systems concept a strong scientific rationale.

One branding issue should be handled immediately. As of October 2026, the official Space Apps team
directory already contains teams using names such as ASTRAHEALTH and ASTRA – Astronaut Self-health
Tracking & Risk Assessment for this challenge.  Keep ASTRA internally, but give the submission a
distinctive subtitle, for example:
ASTRA Command — Autonomous Space Telehealth & Resilience Architecture
or
ASTRA-MED — Earth-Independent Crew Health Intelligence
The technical specification below assumes ASTRA Command as the working product name.
Scientific basis, scope, and assumptions
NASA's Human Research Program organizes the human-spaceflight problem around five hazards: space
radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile/closed
environments. HRP identifies associated risks including altered immune responses, cardiovascular
adaptations, reduced cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness, spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular
effects, bone changes, behavioral-health issues, and inadequate sleep or irregular schedules. 
ASTRA should therefore monitor multiple domains rather than reducing astronaut health to heart rate
alone. At the same time, not everything NASA studies can be measured continuously. Recent human-
spaceflight studies show changes in immune, metabolic, coagulation, oxidative-stress, bone, and molecular
pathways, but much of that evidence comes from laboratory measurements at discrete pre-flight/post-flight
time points rather than wearable real-time telemetry. The Inspiration4 multi-omic study, for example,

observed changes in oxidative-stress, coagulation and other secretome-related signals; a long-duration

NASA OSDR is particularly valuable because it integrates physiological, behavioral, biomedical, bioimaging,
omics and environmental data, while its Biological Data API provides REST and tabular query mechanisms.
Most OSDR data are publicly accessible; NASA notes that processed astronaut-derived data may be publicly
available while sensitive sequence data can be controlled access. 
7
8
3

Two useful human-spaceflight examples are OSD-575, containing Inspiration4 blood-serum metabolic and
immune/cardiac cytokine arrays, and OSD-656, containing an Inspiration4 urine inflammatory-protein
panel. Both are valuable for scientific context and simulator design, but neither should be represented as
live astronaut telemetry. 
NASA's Environmental Data Application includes environmental monitoring such as temperature, humidity,
oxygen, carbon dioxide and radiation, while RadLab provides programmatic access to radiation telemetry.
These are much more appropriate for ASTRA's environmental/radiation layer than trying to invent a “live
NASA medical API.” 
Recent spaceflight research also supports including cognition while emphasizing uncertainty. A 2026 study
demonstrated the feasibility of repeated EEG “brain vital signs” and neuropsychological testing in two
astronauts around a 17-day ISS mission, but the authors explicitly cautioned about the tiny sample size.
ASTRA should therefore offer short reaction-time/cognitive tests as personal longitudinal measurements,
not population-level diagnostic scores. 
Core assumptions for implementation
ID Assumption
A-01 Hackathon demo uses six fictional crew members and no identifiable real astronaut medicalrecord.
A-02 All generated telemetry carries synthetic=true ; replayed public data carries its datasetprovenance and license.
A-03 “Live” means stream-as-received. A low-Earth-orbit demo may appear near-real-time; a Marsprofile must visibly display delayed/stale Earth reception.
A-04 ASTRA is a research/hackathon prototype, not NASA-certified, flight-qualified, clinicallyvalidated, FDA-cleared or a substitute for a flight surgeon/crew medical officer.
A-05 Red status means high-priority review/escalation in the simulated system, not “thisastronaut has disease X.”
A-06 Detection logic works without an LLM. LLMs may explain, summarize and orchestrate restrictedtools but never determine the sole safety-critical alert state.
A-07 The 3D “digital twin” is a data-linked visualization/interaction twin, not a validatedcomputational physiological model.
A-08 Production-like engineering means modular APIs, testing, provenance, security and deploymentdiscipline; it does not imply actual flight certification.
A-09
Pre-event work must stay within the competition/local-event rules applicable to your team. The
official 2026 site describes the project submission period as November 14–15 and encourages
submission of what teams accomplish during the hackathon, so the team should verify its local
rules before pre-building submission-specific code.

The digital twin deserves one explicit design rule: animation follows measurement, not imagination. A
heart-rate value may drive heartbeat animation; an actual ECG replay may synchronize to R-peaks;
respiratory rate may drive a subtle respiratory cycle. An elevated anomaly may highlight the relevant
16

domain. But a heart-rate deviation must not cause ASTRA to visually invent a blocked artery, arrhythmia,
damaged organ or other diagnosis.
For performance, do not serialize every waveform sample as JSON. PhysioNet BIDMC contains ECG, PPG
and respiratory signals sampled at 125 Hz, with HR/RR/SpO₂ numerics at 1 Hz.  For six simulated crew
members, three 125-Hz float32 channels alone are about 0.78 GB/day before metadata/compression.
ASTRA should therefore write waveform data in short binary chunks, retain/stream decimated versions for
visualization, and store scalar/derived features separately.
Recommended rendering hierarchy:
Scene layer: Earth, spacecraft, orbital/communication path, particles.
Interface layer: HTML/DOM cards and charts rather than rendering every piece of text in WebGL.
Twin layer: optimized GLB model, organ/health-region meshes, animated shaders, labels.
Emergency layer: alert halo, evidence lines, body-region focus camera.
Fallback layer: static/2D body map if WebGL2 or GPU performance is insufficient.
The visual objective is NASA Mission Control credibility with premium cinematic transitions, not an
unreadable science-fiction HUD.
Data, AI, testing, and validation
A research-grade project needs a strict boundary between real public research data, replayed waveform
data, and synthetic mission telemetry.
PhysioNet's BIDMC dataset has 53 eight-minute recordings containing PPG, impedance respiration and ECG
at 125 Hz plus HR, respiratory rate and SpO₂ numerics at 1 Hz, but those data came from critically ill hospital
patients. They are useful for waveform structure, artifacts and pipeline testing, not astronaut clinical
calibration.  Sleep-EDF contains 197 whole-night polysomnographic recordings with EEG/EOG/chin
EMG, event markers and expert-scored hypnograms, and is useful for testing sleep-processing components
without pretending that it represents an astronaut population.

Anomaly-detection ladder
Do not begin with an LSTM autoencoder merely because it sounds advanced.
Tier A — mandatory: robust personalized statistics such as median/MAD or rolling robust z-score,
persistence rules, rate-of-change checks and data-quality gating. This is fast, interpretable and easy to
validate.
Tier B — mandatory if time permits: Isolation Forest or similar multivariate unsupervised detector using
normalized deviations, recent trends, activity context and quality indicators.
Tier C — research extension: temporal autoencoder/sequence model only if it materially outperforms
simpler baselines on frozen scenario and public-signal tests.
The combined health status should be a case engine, not one mysterious “AI health score.” Judges
should be able to open any alert and see precisely which observations, baseline deviations, persistence
interval and model version caused it.
Predictive service
Forecasts should say things such as:
“Resting heart-rate trend is projected to remain outside this crew member's recent baseline
over the next six hours if the current trajectory continues.”

The agent should behave as a state machine:
OBSERVE → VERIFY QUALITY → READ BASELINE → EXPLAIN EVENT → RETRIEVE EVIDENCE → 
REQUEST/RECOMMEND SAFE CHECK-IN → DRAFT CASE → HUMAN ACK → TRANSMIT

Prohibited LLM capabilities should include unrestricted shell execution, arbitrary Internet browsing in

declaring a diagnosis, or bypassing human acknowledgement.

independence makes decision-support capability increasingly valuable.  That is excellent justification for

NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is explicitly designed to help teams govern, measure and manage AI
risk across the lifecycle, while NIST SP 800-218A extends secure-software-development practices to AI
systems and models. These provide appropriate non-medical-device governance references for ASTRA's AI
lifecycle. 
The ethical boundary around medical advice must also be explicit. FDA's current CDS policy distinguishes
informational decision support from software that produces specific diagnostic/treatment directives or
supports time-critical clinical decisions, and patient/caregiver-facing functions raise additional regulatory
considerations.  For a hackathon prototype, ASTRA should therefore use language such as “review
required,” “verify measurement,” “perform scheduled assessment,” “consult onboard protocol/
medical officer,” rather than autonomous diagnosis or medication instructions.
ASTRA's README and footer should display:
Research and simulation prototype. Not a medical device. Not NASA-certified or flight-
qualified. Synthetic telemetry is clearly identified. AI output supports review and does
not replace qualified medical judgment.
